ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The physics interest group at our school has decided to hold a remote-controlled car race. The race track is as shown in the figure. The car, which can be considered a point mass, starts from point A and moves along a horizontal straight track for a distance $L$. It then enters a smooth vertical semicircular track with radius $R$ at point B, and must pass through the highest point $C$ of the semicircular track to complete the race. Point B is the lowest point of the semicircular track, and the horizontal straight track is tangent to the semicircular track at point B. The mass of the car is $m=0.5\mathrm{kg}$, and it operates at a rated power of $P=2\mathrm{W}$ after being powered on. Before entering the vertical circular track, the car experiences a constant resistance force of $F_{\mathrm{f}}=0.4\mathrm{N}$. After entering the vertical circular track, the resistance forces can be neglected. The values are $L=10.00\mathrm{m}$, $R=0.32\mathrm{m}$, and $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$. Find:

1. What is the minimum speed required for the racing car at point $C$ on the semicircular track to complete the race?
2. How large must the supporting force be at point $B$ on the semicircular track for the racing car to complete the race?
3. How long must the electric motor operate at least for the racing car to complete the race?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the small car starts from point A on the left side and moves to the right along a horizontal straight track; the length of the horizontal segment is marked as L; after reaching point B, it enters a vertical semicircular track. B is the lowest point of the semicircular track, and the horizontal track is tangent to the circular arc at point B; the upper end of the circular arc is marked as C, and the figure also marks the radius R from the center of the circle to the circular arc. Then reason: 1. When the small car can just pass through the highest point C, the minimum contact condition at the highest point is that the supporting force can just be 0, and at this time gravity provides the centripetal force: mg = m v_C^2 / R. Therefore v_C = sqrt(gR). Substituting g=10 m/s^2, R=0.32 m, gives v_C = sqrt(3.2) = 4sqrt(5)/5 m/s. 2. From B to C, the resistance on the circular arc segment is ignored, and the height from B to C increases by 2R. Conservation of mechanical energy: 1/2 m v_B^2 = 1/2 m v_C^2 + mg(2R). Therefore v_B^2 = v_C^2 + 4gR = gR + 4gR = 5gR. Substituting numerical values gives v_B^2 = 5×10×0.32 = 16. At point B, the centripetal direction is vertically upward, and the force equation is N_B - mg = m v_B^2/R. Substituting m=0.5 kg, g=10 m/s^2, R=0.32 m, v_B^2=16, gives N_B = mg + m v_B^2/R = 5 + 0.5×16/0.32 = 5 + 25 = 30 N. 3. Suppose the small car starts from rest at point A, and the minimum working time of the motor is t. On the horizontal segment from A to B, the motor does work Pt, resistance does negative work F_f L, and when reaching point B it needs at least kinetic energy 1/2 m v_B^2. Therefore Pt - F_f L = 1/2 m v_B^2. Substituting P=2 W, F_f=0.4 N, L=10.00 m, m=0.5 kg, v_B^2=16, gives 2t - 0.4×10 = 1/2×0.5×16 = 4, namely 2t - 4 = 4, so t = 4 s.
